# Documentation as Executable Foundations — Research Draft 10
URL: https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/drafts/10-documentation-as-executable-foundations/
Status: research-draft
Conceptual source: Valto Loikkanen

# Documentation as Executable Foundations

*Durable meaning from which implementations and behavior can be derived*


**Conceptual source and direction: Valto Loikkanen.** Research and drafting: Codex (OpenAI), at his request. Research draft 1.0 · 26 November 2026.

## Abstract

Valto Loikkanen places documentation, terminology, capability requirements and governing decisions among the relatively durable foundations of adaptive software. This paper explains how documentation can shape execution without being mistaken for executable code or a grant of authority. It develops a source-to-realization model, identifies semantic categories that prevent accidental policy changes, and describes how shared guidance can bound intelligent interpretation when a case is not predefined. The contribution is operational reliance on attributable meaning rather than on a particular implementation. [S01]

## 1. Documentation can precede the implementation

Documentation often describes a system after it has been built. In an adaptive architecture, it also defines what should remain true when the system is generated or changed.

A capability's purpose, information semantics, acceptable result and boundaries can persist through a UI redesign, a backend rewrite or a shift between agentic and deterministic execution. These documents give different actors a common basis for understanding and realization.

The phrase executable foundations refers to this operational role. It does not imply that ordinary prose is automatically executable or that every instruction-like sentence should be obeyed by an agent.

## 2. Identify what kind of statement is being read

| Statement class | Function | Consequence of confusion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fact | Reports something established by a source | May be mistaken for a requirement |
| Purpose | Explains the capability's meaningful outcome | May be replaced by an implementation detail |
| Rule | States a binding invariant within its authority | May be weakened into a preference |
| Default | Supplies normal behavior when no choice overrides it | May become an unnecessary veto |
| Example | Illustrates a case | May become a universal requirement |
| Inference | Proposes an interpretation | May be promoted into accepted truth |
| Unknown | Preserves unresolved meaning | May be silently filled with invention |

CRD's public documentation explicitly distinguishes such categories and separates a capability from its realizations. That separation supports consistent intelligent use of documents while retaining uncertainty. [S09]

## 3. Capability meaning and operational realization

For a commitment-history capability, the durable description might define what qualifies as an accepted commitment, what constitutes a meaningful result and how disputed evidence is handled. A realization might use a graph, a query or an agent that reads source records.

A capability document should not be enlarged to include every internal helper. It should identify a complete, meaningful ability. Operational documentation then records the selected implementation, dependencies, exposure and acceptance evidence.

This preserves a common semantic middle between product rationale, user interaction, API descriptions, tools and code. Domain-specific documents remain useful. The capability reference connects them rather than replacing them.

## 4. A derivation chain

`attributable sources → controlled terminology → capability meaning → interaction → realization → acceptance evidence`

Each transition needs traceability appropriate to its consequence. A realization should identify the source revision it implements. An acceptance case should test a meaningful requirement, rather than merely mirror the generated code.

The chain is not one-way. Actual use can reveal a missing definition or a conflict. The system can propose a revision, but the revision should pass through the relevant source authority rather than quietly become a rule because one implementation used it.

PROV-DM provides a vocabulary for relating source entities, transformation activities and responsible agents. It supports traceability; it does not replace the authority process that accepts a change. [S17]

## 5. Shared principles can govern unspecified cases

No useful documentation predicts every situation. Loikkanen proposes that strong foundations can also define where to look for relevant guidance and how to apply it when a case is not predefined. [S01]

A bounded agent can use an accepted glossary, documented defaults, domain references and capability boundaries to resolve ordinary gaps. This can keep custom behavior limited even when interactions emerge dynamically.

The scope of inference matters. An agent may choose a readable layout under design guidance or select an existing retrieval method. It should not invent an accepted business definition, erase an explicit unknown or infer a new permission from an example.

The foundation is therefore both information and a disciplined method of interpretation. An unset detail need not stop every action, but a material unresolved question must remain visible.

## 6. Schemas as projections of meaning

A schema can be generated from shared capability and information semantics. It can represent the fields, types and operations needed for a particular interaction without becoming the ultimate authority over their meaning.

The same capability may have a natural-language description, a GraphQL view, an HTTP exposure or an event representation. Their technical contracts must be appropriate to their consumers. The durable documentation records which meanings and rules these views must preserve. [S11, S13, S16]

This supports the language-and-format framing: documentation supplies the context that lets participants interpret different expressions coherently. It reduces the need to create a custom semantic world for every format.

## 7. Authority and source order

Accessible documentation is not necessarily governing documentation. A retrieved webpage can describe a technique without authorizing its use. A copied policy may be outdated. A worker's note may be a proposal rather than an accepted owner decision.

The system needs to identify the declared source, applicable version and authority of material statements. It should distinguish permission to edit a document from permission to activate its proposed policy.

PIOS's public account separates source authority, information-system membership and implementation placement. EIOS similarly records entity governance and decision roles. These supply relevant context for deriving behavior from documents without confusing a local copy with canonical authority. [S07, S08]

## 8. Failure modes and evaluation

Documentation can be incomplete, contradictory, hard to retrieve or too costly to maintain. Agents can confidently reconcile conflicts incorrectly. Generated implementations can pass superficial tests while implementing the wrong category of statement.

Evaluate whether independent realizations preserve the same capability meaning. Give them normal cases, exceptions, explicit unknowns and conflicting defaults. Ask whether each conclusion is traceable to a source and whether a material new decision is clearly identified.

A useful change test revises one governing rule, then checks which realizations and interactions must change. This examines actual dependency management rather than merely counting document coverage.

## 9. Contribution and practical adoption

Start with a capability whose meaning is repeatedly lost between documents, interfaces and code. Preserve its existing source context, identify material semantic categories and derive one additional realization. Keep the document small enough to use and explicit enough to prevent known ambiguity.

The contribution is durable, attributable meaning that can guide several implementations. Documentation becomes an operational asset when actors can find it, interpret it correctly and demonstrate that the resulting behavior preserves its intended boundaries.


## Sources and attribution

**[S07]** peecos / Valto Loikkanen. *PIOS 2.0 master and public README*. PIOS 2.0; retrieved 26 November 2026. [Original source](https://www.peecos.org/pios/master).

**[S08]** Entity Core / Valto Loikkanen. *EIOS 1.0, Keel, and Weave*. Working master v1.4, 21 November 2026. [Original source](https://github.com/entity-core/eios/blob/main/spec/eios-1.0-master-documentation.md).

**[S09]** Valto Loikkanen. *Capability Documentation / Capability Requirements Document framework*. Draft 0.4; package 0.8.0. [Original source](https://valto.github.io/crd/specification.html).

**[S11]** GraphQL Foundation / specification contributors. *GraphQL Specification*. September 2025 edition, selected explicitly. [Original source](https://spec.graphql.org/September2025/).

**[S13]** OpenAPI Initiative. *OpenAPI Specification*. Version 3.1.1, 24 October 2024; selected explicitly. [Original source](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.1.html).

# Individuals and Entities as Information Endpoints — Research Draft 11
URL: https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/drafts/11-individuals-and-entities-as-information-endpoints/
Status: research-draft
Conceptual source: Valto Loikkanen

# Individuals and Entities as Information Endpoints

*Separating the principal from the actor and the serving implementation*


**Conceptual source and direction: Valto Loikkanen.** Research and drafting: Codex (OpenAI), at his request. Research draft 1.0 · 26 November 2026.

## Abstract

Valto Loikkanen proposes individuals and entities as the persistent principals of an information architecture. Humans, agents and applications act directly or indirectly on their behalf, while implementations serve their needs through changing interfaces. This paper interprets the two-principal model as an architectural organizing choice, rather than a claim that every network endpoint fits a simple ownership ontology. It develops the separation of principal, requester, beneficiary, information authority and realization, including shared records and cross-principal interaction. [S01]

## 1. Who persists when the software changes?

A person may replace a notes application, an agent provider or a hosting service. An organization may replace employees, dashboards or communication tools. Its information, relationships and commitments should not disappear with each replacement.

The proposed architecture anchors continuity in the individual or entity served. PIOS describes a personal information foundation; EIOS describes an entity information foundation. These are public framework models with related principles and distinct scope. Their documentation does not establish universal adoption or production readiness. [S07, S08]

An endpoint in this paper means a logical point of information continuity and governed interaction. It need not be one server, address, physical machine or database.

## 2. Principal, actor and implementation are independent

| Dimension | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Principal | The individual or entity whose authorized purpose is served | Person, company, association |
| Operational actor | Who initiates or performs an interaction | Human, agent, application |
| Beneficiary | Who ultimately benefits from the work | Principal, customer, member or another party |
| Information authority | Who can accept or govern the relevant record | Owner, designated entity role, shared decision process |
| Realization | How the receiver fulfills the need | Agentic, deterministic or hybrid execution |

No dimension automatically determines another. An application may request information for a person and receive agentic fulfillment. An agent may request information for an entity and receive a direct query result. A human may act under an entity role rather than in a personal capacity.

The immediate actor's identity therefore cannot substitute for the represented principal or the scope of delegated authority.

## 3. Two principal categories, many practical arrangements

The model distinguishes individuals from entities to preserve personal and organizational continuity. It does not imply that entities have one simple human decision-maker or that all information has a single owner.

An organization can contain roles, teams, jurisdictions and conflicting interests. A shared agreement may belong to several participants' records. A public dataset may be served by infrastructure whose operator and data authority differ.

These arrangements can be represented through relationships among principals, roles and records. If an autonomous agent participates without a clear represented principal, the system should preserve that uncertainty or identify the accountable operator; it should not invent a human owner to force the case into the model.

The distinction is useful if it clarifies authority and continuity. It should be extended or qualified where it conceals them.

## 4. Direct and indirect needs

A human may explicitly ask an agent to retrieve a document. An agent may also discover that it needs a supporting record to accomplish an already authorized objective. The second request serves an indirect need.

Indirect work does not require a new human instruction for every internal dependency. It does require the dependency to remain within the purpose and scope of the existing delegation. A task to prepare an internal briefing does not automatically authorize external contact or disclosure.

The interaction context should therefore identify the requesting actor, represented principal, purpose, applicable grant and intended result recipient. The exact representation can vary by language and format, provided the meaning remains clear enough for the consequences involved.

## 5. Cross-principal relationships

The proposed model supports individual-to-individual, individual-to-entity and entity-to-entity interactions. Their information exchanges may use ordinary human communication, applications, agents or combinations.

PAIX's public guidance explores addressable human and agent participation, disclosure and optional channel upgrades. It explicitly separates advertising a capability from granting access. A2A and other mechanisms can supply particular execution and task interactions. [S10, S15]

An exchange should preserve each participant's independent policy. Agreement on a language or format does not override either party's authority boundaries, and a receiving system's access does not entitle it to disclose the information elsewhere.

## 6. Shared information and accepted state

One record can have several legitimate views and custodians. A signed agreement, for example, may appear in both an individual's and an entity's information foundations. These are not automatically competing masters; they can preserve the same source identity with distinct governance context.

The important questions are which record is authoritative for which purpose, how accepted changes are represented, and what each participant is entitled to retain or modify. Copying a record does not transfer every right associated with it.

Provenance can relate originals, copies, derived assertions and actions across systems. An acceptance process must still determine which statements or revisions count as agreed. [S17]

## 7. Replacing an operational actor

A provider change should preserve the principal's information, accepted commitments, relevant grants and operational history. Credentials and permissions may require separate re-establishment; exporting content does not export authority automatically.

A new agent should be able to understand the current capability and decision context without inheriting unsupported claims from a former actor. The principal retains continuity even when the representation and execution change.

Local-first and Solid research provide relevant approaches to user control and separation of information from applications. Their technical approaches and governance scope differ from PIOS and EIOS; they are comparison points rather than interchangeable implementations. [S05, S29]

## 8. Evaluation and contribution

Test a workflow across a change of actor or implementation. Can the system preserve record identity, accepted state, source attribution and the correct represented principal? Can it distinguish personal work from entity work and refuse an out-of-scope request?

Include shared records, role changes and revoked delegation. Ask whether the human participants can explain who is represented and who is entitled to decide.

The contribution is a persistent principal model that separates purpose and information continuity from replaceable actors and software. Its value is practical clarity about who is served, what persists and how legitimate interaction continues when tools change.


## Sources and attribution

**[S05]** Martin Kleppmann, Adam Wiggins, Peter van Hardenberg and Mark McGranaghan. *Local-first software: You own your data, in spite of the cloud*. Web essay April 2019; Onward! October 2019, pp. 154–178; DOI 10.1145/3359591.3359737. [Original source](https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/).

**[S07]** peecos / Valto Loikkanen. *PIOS 2.0 master and public README*. PIOS 2.0; retrieved 26 November 2026. [Original source](https://www.peecos.org/pios/master).

**[S08]** Entity Core / Valto Loikkanen. *EIOS 1.0, Keel, and Weave*. Working master v1.4, 21 November 2026. [Original source](https://github.com/entity-core/eios/blob/main/spec/eios-1.0-master-documentation.md).

**[S10]** Private AI Exchange / PAIX. *Human & Agent Interoperability*. Non-normative design guidance for PAIX v0.1. [Original source](https://github.com/privateaiexchange/paix-spec/blob/main/docs/Human_Agent_Interoperability.md).

# The Lifecycle of Liquid Software — Research Draft 12
URL: https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/drafts/12-the-lifecycle-of-liquid-software/
Status: research-draft
Conceptual source: Valto Loikkanen

# The Lifecycle of Liquid Software

*Emergence, specialization, consolidation and retirement without losing capability meaning*


**Conceptual source and direction: Valto Loikkanen.** Research and drafting: Codex (OpenAI), at his request. Research draft 1.0 · 26 November 2026.

## Abstract

Liquid Software requires an operational lifecycle, not merely the ability to generate code. Valto Loikkanen proposes reversible movement among agentic, hybrid and deterministic realizations according to demand and constraints. This paper defines lifecycle states, transition evidence and the difference between retiring an implementation and withdrawing a capability. It addresses seasonal demand, dependency drift, user familiarity and preservation of accepted information. The resulting model makes adaptability manageable while allowing stable implementations to remain stable when they provide the best value. [S01]

## 1. A population of implementations

An information capability can have several realizations. A general agent may handle novel cases; a query may serve a stable pattern; a temporary interface may support a workshop; a hybrid route may handle exceptions.

Treating these as a population makes different lifetimes visible. Some implementations are short-lived, some recurring and some effectively permanent. The capability's identity and meaningful outcome can persist across them.

The lifecycle should not force a linear march from agent to software. Demand, information and constraints can change in either direction.

## 2. Capability lifecycle and implementation lifecycle differ

Retiring a specialized query can leave the capability available through another route. Withdrawing the capability means the system no longer promises the relevant outcome. These are different decisions.

A replacement must preserve the applicable contract or explicitly revise it. If the fallback is slower, less complete or less reliable, the system should determine whether it still meets the accepted capability conditions.

Accepted records, pending work and commitments also have their own lifecycles. Their retention cannot be inferred from the lifespan of the software that created or displayed them.

## 3. Proposed realization states

| State | Meaning | Evidence needed to leave the state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Candidate | Proposed response to an actual need | Clear scope and expected value |
| Experimental | Isolated construction or evaluation | Relevant correctness and boundary evidence |
| Shadow | Compared with an accepted route | Adequate behavior on new cases |
| Active | Available for a declared request class | Current dependencies and runtime assurance |
| Restricted | Temporarily limited or bypassed | Cause resolved or scope explicitly revised |
| Retired | No longer selected for execution | Capability disposition and evidence retained |

These states are a reference design, not a claim about the lifecycle of any existing PIOS component. A small temporary renderer may need fewer explicit stages than a shared state-changing service.

## 4. What justifies a transition?

Emergence follows an unmet or newly expressed need. Specialization follows demonstrated repeated value and adequate semantic stability. Consolidation follows evidence that several realizations share behavior without losing distinctions. Retirement follows declining value, superseded assumptions or an accepted replacement.

Demand alone is insufficient. The decision also depends on quality, latency, resource cost, security, source coverage, recovery and human effort. A rarely used critical route may remain valuable. A heavily used route may need restriction if its assumptions are wrong.

The optimizer should preserve the reason for a material transition. Without that history, future actors may repeat failed adaptations or mistake a retired artifact for a currently accepted implementation.

## 5. Identity, dependencies and acceptance

A realization should identify the capability and interaction version it supports, its own construction provenance, relevant dependencies and accepted operating scope. Code generated by an agent can still run deterministically; construction method does not determine runtime control.

CRD explicitly separates capability meaning, interaction contracts and realizations. Its runtime distinctions help prevent agent-built software from being treated as agent-controlled execution. [S09]

Acceptance evidence should follow the meaningful boundary. It can include source-backed cases, denied scope, changed source revisions and recovery. Repeat testing only when the relevant inputs or unresolved risks change; a renamed artifact alone does not establish a new correctness question.

## 6. Seasonal return and dependency drift

A annual reporting capability might use a specialized route for a short period. After the period, the route may retire from active operation while its source, scope and evidence remain available under retention policy.

When the need returns, reinstatement should check current terminology, source structure, permissions and operational dependencies. Historical success is useful evidence, but it may not prove compatibility with changed conditions.

The same applies to model-driven components. Changing an extraction model may alter derived assertions even if the source bytes remain unchanged. A realization must be evaluated against the requirement that actually depends on that model.

## 7. Stability is sometimes the optimum

Users learn interfaces and develop reliable habits. Continuous visible change can impose cognitive costs even when generation is cheap. A stable view may therefore remain preferred while the serving implementation evolves behind it.

Malleable-software research emphasizes users' ability to reshape their environment. That is compatible with choosing to keep a useful environment unchanged. The lifecycle should support control over adaptation, including the choice to retain a familiar form. [S04]

Likewise, a proven backend may remain cheaper than regenerating it. Liquid capability is the ability to adapt appropriately, not a requirement to demonstrate change at every opportunity.

## 8. Retirement and recovery

Before retirement, identify ongoing requests, external commitments, accepted state and pending work. Stop selecting the route through the supported mechanism; preserve the information required to understand and recover relevant outcomes.

Retirement should not silently delete originals or invalidate a client's agreed interaction. If the capability is being withdrawn, communicate its disposition through the appropriate decision and interaction process.

End-to-end reasoning is especially useful during replacement: a component may exit cleanly while a client still cannot determine whether its operation completed. The retained outcome and recovery boundary matter more than the component's local success. [S20]

## 9. Evaluation and open questions

Run a changing workload through several realizations. Compare stable service, selective adaptation and aggressive adaptation. Measure useful fulfillment, maintenance cost, regressions, user learning, fallback quality and recovery.

Test a withdrawal during work, a seasonal return, a capability revision and consolidation of superficially similar patterns. Determine whether accepted information and meaningful distinctions survive.

The contribution is a reversible lifecycle around durable capability meaning. It makes generation, specialization and retirement parts of one accountable process rather than independent acts of software creation and deletion.


## Sources and attribution

**[S01]** Valto Loikkanen and ChatGPT. *Define liquid software — shared conversation*. Retrieved 26 November 2026. [Original source](https://chatgpt.com/share/6b077626-c894-83ed-aabf-d21a363c4313).

**[S04]** Geoffrey Litt, Josh Horowitz, Peter van Hardenberg and Todd Matthews. *Malleable Software: Restoring User Agency in a World of Locked-Down Apps*. June 2025. [Original source](https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/malleable-software/).

**[S09]** Valto Loikkanen. *Capability Documentation / Capability Requirements Document framework*. Draft 0.4; package 0.8.0. [Original source](https://valto.github.io/crd/specification.html).

**[S20]** J. H. Saltzer, D. P. Reed and D. D. Clark. *End-to-End Arguments in System Design*. ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2(4), November 1984, pp. 277–288. [Original source](https://web.mit.edu/Saltzer/www/publications/endtoend/endtoend.pdf).

Valto Loikkanen supplies the conceptual synthesis and directs this collection. Codex prepared the research and prose. # The Internet Beyond Applications — Research Draft 13
URL: https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/drafts/13-the-internet-beyond-applications/
Status: research-draft
Conceptual source: Valto Loikkanen

# The Internet Beyond Applications

*Activities, information flows and economic relationships beneath the software layer*


**Conceptual source and direction: Valto Loikkanen.** Research and drafting: Codex (OpenAI), at his request. Research draft 1.0 · 26 November 2026.

## Abstract

Valto Loikkanen's Internet on One Page model describes activities, actors, information flows and revenue arrangements without making a particular application the organizing center. This paper uses the supplied diagram, the eleven-page November 2026 conceptual whitepaper and the shared discussion to examine how adaptive interaction and Liquid Software could serve those underlying relationships. It distinguishes a conceptual economic map from legal classifications and market predictions. The principal research question is whether adaptable implementation can increase effective choice and value creation while information ownership, human authority and market incentives remain explicit. [S01, S02]

## 1. What the diagram makes visible

The Internet on One Page identifies seven activities: create, control, promote, connect, discover, acquire and consume. It shows humans, AI agents and organizations exchanging information, with several information categories and economic arrangements beneath the activity sequence.

Applications are not the fundamental categories of the map. A particular application may support several activities, while the same activity may be performed through several tools or participants. This makes the model useful for considering a digital economy in which interfaces and implementations change more readily.

<figure class="wide-figure"><img src="/liquid/assets/internet-on-one-page.jpg" alt="The Internet on One Page: seven activities above exchanges among humans, agents and organizations, with information categories and five revenue models below."><figcaption>Figure 1. The Internet on One Page. Original diagram extracted from page 1 of the owner-supplied November 2026 whitepaper. Valto Loikkanen is identified as originator and source of the framework. The earlier creation date of the diagram is not established.</figcaption></figure>

The supplied whitepaper distinguishes direct human participation from delegated agent operation across the same infrastructure. Its two interconnected internets are functional perspectives, rather than separate physical networks or an obligatory replacement of human experiences. It also separates information owners, objective setters, decision makers, operational actors and beneficiaries. These distinctions explain why changing an interface need not change who controls the relationship. [S02, pp. 4, 7–9]

## 2. Activities as durable capability categories

| Activity | Underlying concern | Adaptive possibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create | Produce information, knowledge or an offering | Compose appropriate tools around the current need |
| Control | Govern information, use and authority | Preserve decisions across changing implementations |
| Promote | Communicate availability and value | Adapt communication to the audience and context |
| Connect | Establish relationships and interaction | Choose a mutually suitable language and channel |
| Discover | Find relevant information and capabilities | Combine intelligent discovery with precise access |
| Acquire | Obtain an offering, right or access | Support an agreed transaction through different forms |
| Consume | Use information or capability for a purpose | Present and execute in a contextually useful way |

These are broad categories, not seven mandatory software modules or complete CRDs. A particular capability should still be defined at a meaningful operational scope.

## 3. Information categories and their limits

The diagram associates promotional information with attention value, public-domain information with free value, owned information with monetary value, and private or personal information with personal and targeting value. [S02]

These labels are a conceptual map of economic roles, not mutually exclusive legal categories. Owned information can be freely shared; personal information can have commercial relevance; and publicly accessible material is not necessarily public domain. The proposed architecture must keep actual rights, purpose and permission explicit rather than infer them from a diagram label.

Adaptive presentation does not alter the underlying permission. An agent that can summarize valuable information is not automatically entitled to acquire, disclose or monetize it.

## 4. Revenue models can outlast interfaces

| Arrangement in the diagram | Relationship | What remains important as software changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Licensing | Licensor and licensee | Scope, permitted use and attribution |
| Advertising | Advertiser and channel | Incentives, disclosure and attention allocation |
| Transaction fees | Broker and parties | Service responsibility and transaction outcome |
| Commerce | Seller and buyer | Offering, payment and accepted commitment |
| Subscriptions | Provider and subscriber | Ongoing entitlement and continuity |

An adaptive system can support these relationships through a website, message exchange, application or agent interaction. The economic arrangement still requires understandable terms and accepted effects.

The disappearance of a dedicated marketplace screen would not eliminate market power, liability or bargaining. These concerns can move into discovery, identity, data access, payment or agent selection.

## 5. An illustrative exchange

A person wants an analysis using a specialist dataset. Their representative discovers an available offering, identifies applicable terms, obtains permitted access and delivers an appropriate result. The seller may fulfill the need through an existing query or intelligent assembly.

The interaction could use a human-readable channel, a structured request or a negotiated combination. A dedicated application is optional in the example; the parties, rights, meaning and accepted transaction are not.

This is a proposed scenario. It does not establish legal enforceability, market adoption or technical interoperability among current systems.

## 6. Independence, representation and incentives

An agent can act for a principal while also depending on a provider whose incentives differ. The principal should be able to understand who operates the agent, what interests it serves and when it receives compensation or preferential information.

The conversation mentions a Personal Intelligence Fiduciary as a complementary idea. Here it is a design question about loyal representation and conflicts of interest, not an assertion that an AI service has a legally established fiduciary status. The supplied whitepaper similarly identifies interest alignment as a requirement and distinguishes an agent's operational ability from its authority to act. [S01, S02, pp. 9–10]

Cheaper customization does not itself protect the customer's interests. A system can generate a personalized interface that strongly favors its operator. Effective agency requires information continuity, clear delegation, relevant transparency and a practical way to replace the representative.

## 7. Open interaction and concentration

PAIX explores an open entry and fallback channel with explicit optional upgrades. Solid and local-first work explore ways to separate user information and control from applications. These are relevant design comparisons, not evidence that an independent market will automatically emerge. [S10, S29, S05]

Liquid Software could reduce some barriers to specialized service creation. It could also increase dependence on a few providers of intelligence, trusted context or distribution. The key empirical issue is where control and switching costs move.

An open interface is useful only if participants can actually use it under workable terms, preserve their information and retain responsibility for accepted commitments.

The supplied whitepaper proposes evaluating intermediaries by their distinct contributions: navigation, information aggregation, trust, transaction coordination and market access. Agents may alter the value of navigation while leaving verification or physical delivery valuable. A useful comparison therefore follows the service each intermediary performs and who benefits, rather than treating an entire platform category as destined to disappear. These remain analytical propositions; the supplied document explicitly reports no external research or empirical validation. [S02, pp. 9–11]

## 8. Research questions

Evaluate a bounded exchange across several presentation and implementation choices. Can the parties discover the offering, understand terms, determine authority, complete the transaction and preserve the result? What happens when a participant changes its agent or software provider?

Measure total transaction cost, comprehension, failures, switching effort, supplier choice and distribution of benefit. Include situations where conventional platforms provide superior trust or coordination.

Longer-term claims require observing real market behavior. Faster interface creation alone does not establish increased competition or reduced concentration.

## 9. Contribution

The Internet on One Page provides an economic and information-flow context for the technical papers. Its activities and relationships can remain recognizable while the software serving them changes.

The contribution of the combined argument is to ask which parts of the economy are fundamental commitments among principals and which are contingent implementation arrangements. That distinction can guide research without assuming that software flexibility dissolves the institutions needed for exchange.

**[S02]** Valto Loikkanen, originator and conceptual source. *The Internet on One Page: A conceptual framework for understanding the internet as an information and value exchange system in the age of AI agents*. Conceptual whitepaper, November 2026; eleven pages; supplied 26 November 2026. The document describes its prose as an AI-assisted elaboration. Original diagram on page 1.

**[S05]** Martin Kleppmann, Adam Wiggins, Peter van Hardenberg and Mark McGranaghan. *Local-first software: You own your data, in spite of the cloud*. Web essay April 2019; Onward! October 2019, pp. 154–178; DOI 10.1145/3359591.3359737. [Original source](https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/).

**[S10]** Private AI Exchange / PAIX. *Human & Agent Interoperability*. Non-normative design guidance for PAIX v0.1. [Original source](https://github.com/privateaiexchange/paix-spec/blob/main/docs/Human_Agent_Interoperability.md).

**[S29]** Solid Community Group. *Solid Protocol*. Draft Community Group Report, 12 May 2024. [Original source](https://solidproject.org/TR/protocol).

# From Software-Centric to Information-Centric Computing — Research Draft 14
URL: https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/drafts/14-from-software-centric-to-information-centric-computing/
Status: research-draft
Conceptual source: Valto Loikkanen

# From Software-Centric to Information-Centric Computing

*A transition that preserves source authority while changing the working environment*


**Conceptual source and direction: Valto Loikkanen.** Research and drafting: Codex (OpenAI), at his request. Research draft 1.0 · 26 November 2026.

## Abstract

Information-centric computing makes information identity, provenance, capability meaning and human authority more durable than a particular application. Valto Loikkanen's synthesis suggests reversing several historical dependencies: capture should preserve useful evidence, presentation should follow context, and implementation should follow actual need. This paper examines how existing systems can move toward that model incrementally. It distinguishes source preservation from bulk accumulation, information continuity from a single database, and a successful export from a proven replacement. [S01]

## 1. The application as both tool and container

An application often bundles information, permissions, presentation and operational logic. This can provide a coherent product, but it can also make the user's information dependent on the product's lifecycle and choices.

The transition proposed here separates these concerns enough to preserve continuity while retaining useful applications. A particular interface may remain the best working surface. The information system should nevertheless know what the records mean, where they came from and how they can survive a change of surface.

Information-centric does not mean interface-free or code-free. It identifies what should retain authority and identity as tools evolve.

## 2. Three dependencies to reconsider

| Current dependency | Transition question |
| --- | --- |
| Capture is limited to anticipated fields | What original evidence should survive beyond current queries? |
| Presentation determines the accessible information | Can the same source support contextually different views? |
| A dedicated implementation precedes every useful activity | Can a bounded intelligent capability serve the emerging need? |

These are questions about priorities, not universal descriptions of every historical system. Many existing systems already separate logical information, storage and views. Codd's data-independence argument is an important antecedent. [S18]

The opportunity is to extend that separation across the user's information, interactions and evolving implementations, rather than treating it only as a database optimization.

## 3. Declare what is authoritative

Before changing a workflow, identify original records, accepted revisions, governing documents, derived assertions and pending work. Record which source is authoritative for each purpose.

A retrieved summary is not automatically an accepted revision. An export is not automatically the new source of truth. A cache may contain pending work that has never been accepted elsewhere. Losing that distinction can create competing masters or delete the only copy of an intended change.

PIOS's public framework separates canonical Core, native processing and retrieval, external applications and physical placement. EIOS distinguishes originals, knowledge and use. These illustrate how logical boundaries can remain explicit even within one deployment. [S07, S08]

## 4. A bounded adoption unit

Choose one capability and a defined information set. For example, let a user browse and revise a selected class of notes through an additional working surface while preserving original identity, revision history and conflict handling.

The required boundary includes full-content readback, meaningful updates, source attribution, acceptance, replay handling and recovery. A successful screen demonstration proves only part of this boundary.

This is a hypothetical adoption example. The paper does not authorize a migration, assert that a particular product supports it, or change an existing owner's source authority.

## 5. Preservation without indiscriminate accumulation

Source preservation should follow purpose and retention choices. Rich material can support new interpretation, but retaining every available file does not guarantee useful context.

Microsoft's MyLifeBits research offers a historical comparison: lifetime personal storage and richer annotation were pursued alongside SQL Server-based retrieval. It illustrates that rich preservation and relational access can coexist. It does not prove that preserving all possible information is desirable or that every future question becomes answerable. [S27]

The transition should retain appropriate originals, record their context and make derived interpretations attributable. It should also identify material deliberately excluded or no longer retained.

## 6. Portability needs more than bytes

An information package can contain files yet fail to preserve meaning. Relationships, accepted state, source versions, annotations and pending revisions may be needed to reconstruct the useful capability.

Likewise, a provider change may require re-establishing credentials and delegated authority. A content export should not imply that access grants or external commitments have automatically transferred.

Local-first research provides important principles for ownership, longevity and usable offline work. Its design emphasis differs from a server-packaged information system, but the continuity test is relevant: can useful work survive the loss or replacement of the current service? [S05]

## 7. Introduce adaptability where it serves a real need

Once the selected information and capability boundary are reliable, add one contextual presentation or retrieval route. Preserve the conventional route as a baseline where useful.

Observe whether the new route improves a meaningful outcome. Repeated needs may justify specialization. A novel question may remain best served through intelligent interpretation. The system should permit both without promoting a derived view into authority.

Documentation and capability requirements can maintain shared meaning through these changes. Their revisions should follow the relevant source authority rather than be inferred from whatever the latest implementation happens to do. [S09]

## 8. Acceptance, recovery and eventual replacement

Acceptance should cover the selected user's actual outcome: information is readable, intended changes are accepted correctly, conflicts remain safe, and the capability can be recovered. Source release or deletion is a later decision supported by the relevant verification and authority.

An isolated reconstruction is useful evidence. It should demonstrate recovery from the retained authoritative package, not depend silently on the original live application's cache.

End-to-end design reasoning explains why component-level success is insufficient. The meaningful outcome may cross source acceptance, network delivery and user acknowledgement. [S20]

## 9. Evaluation and contribution

Measure continuity across a change of working surface or implementation, including semantic fidelity, conflict behavior, recovery effort and user comprehension. Compare the transition cost with actual gains in use and flexibility.

The contribution is a gradual transition model that preserves source authority while reducing application dependence. It provides a path between an ambitious information-centric vision and a bounded useful capability, without requiring a whole-world migration before any benefit can be realized.


## Sources and attribution

# The Architecture of an Intelligence-Native World — Research Draft 15
URL: https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/drafts/15-the-architecture-of-an-intelligence-native-world/
Status: research-draft
Conceptual source: Valto Loikkanen

# The Architecture of an Intelligence-Native World

*A composable reference model for continuity, interaction, execution and human authority*


**Conceptual source and direction: Valto Loikkanen.** Research and drafting: Codex (OpenAI), at his request. Research draft 1.0 · 26 November 2026.

## Abstract

This paper synthesizes Valto Loikkanen's complementary concepts into a reference architecture. Individuals and entities provide persistent principals; information foundations preserve evidence and accepted state; documentation and CRDs supply capability meaning; adaptive interfaces express needs through suitable languages and formats; agentic, deterministic and hybrid realizations fulfill them; and an optimization loop responds to actual demand. Human decision freedom governs all layers. The architecture is a research proposal that can be adopted selectively, not a new mandatory standard or a claim that the complete system is already deployed. [S01]

## 1. What the architecture must accomplish

A useful architecture should let a principal preserve information, express an emerging need, obtain an attributable result and retain control over consequential effects. It should also permit changing the actor, interface or realization without unnecessarily losing capability meaning or accepted state.

These goals create a linked set of concerns. Preserving raw material without meaning is insufficient; shared meaning without accessible evidence is insufficient; flexible execution without authority is unacceptable; and stable information without usable presentation is of limited practical value.

The reference model connects these concerns while allowing existing systems to supply particular components.

## 2. The composable model

| Concern | Reference role | Complementary concepts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Principal | Individual or entity served by an interaction | PIOS, EIOS, personal application ecosystems |
| Information continuity | Originals, accepted revisions, history and provenance | Capture for Unknown Future Value |
| Semantic foundation | Terms, capabilities, rules, defaults and unknowns | Documentation, CRD |
| Interaction | Context, intent, language, format and result | Adaptive Interface, optional PAIX/MCP/A2A exposures |
| Fulfillment | Select and execute an appropriate realization | Intelligence-first, Liquid Software |
| Access optimization | Find and assemble information efficiently | Adaptive Information Retrieval |
| Evolution | Observe, specialize, revise and retire | Self-Optimizing Information System |
| Human authority | Set and revise the effective decision space | Degrees of Decision Freedom |

These are logical responsibilities, not mandatory separate machines or services. A small deployment may combine several; a distributed deployment may separate them. Physical placement should follow the actual framework and task boundary.

## 3. Principal and information foundations

PIOS supplies a public personal information framework; EIOS supplies a related entity framework. They distinguish durable information and governance from the changing tools used to access and apply it. Their published specifications are design sources and should not be treated as independent evidence of every proposed feature. [S07, S08]

The information foundation should preserve original identity, accepted revision and relevant source history. Derived assertions remain attributable. Structured originals and multimodal originals can coexist; the storage medium does not decide authority.

Operational actors may be humans, agents or applications. Their identities, represented principals and grants should remain distinguishable. A component's access or physical proximity does not make it a canonical writer.

## 4. Shared meaning constrains interpretation

Terminology and capability documentation define what participants mean and what a useful result must preserve. They can also provide defaults and methods for resolving ordinary unspecified details.

CRD is relevant because it separates complete capability meaning, interaction behavior and realization. It can connect human-facing and machine-facing forms without making an endpoint or tool the entire capability. [S09]

Unknowns must remain visible. An agent may infer a presentation choice within guidance while lacking authority to redefine a disputed business concept. The architecture needs an explicit route for a real new decision, alongside room for routine interpretation.

## 5. The interaction lifecycle

1. A requester expresses a need using a suitable language or format.
2. The receiver resolves context, represented principal, meaning and expected result.
3. Existing documentation and defaults settle ordinary details where sufficient.
4. The receiver identifies source availability and applicable authority.
5. A suitable realization retrieves information or performs the authorized effect.
6. The result preserves material evidence, uncertainty and accepted state.
7. Selected operational observations inform later optimization.

This sequence is conceptual. A real implementation may combine steps or use an already accepted interaction. It should not introduce negotiation for details that existing shared foundations already resolve.

## 6. Languages, formats and emerging contracts

Natural language, structured queries, diagrams and machine messages are different ways to express or carry the interaction. Shared meaning can precede a dedicated interface.

A schema may be generated for a selected view, inferred under documented conventions or negotiated where exact consumption requires it. The requester proposes the desired information and form; the receiver resolves these against supported meaning, evidence and authority. Existing GraphQL conformance requires its applicable type-system and validation rules, while the broader architecture can support other languages and guarantees. [S11]

REST-style, MCP, A2A and event-driven exposures can provide useful interaction machinery. PAIX's guidance adds a proposed entry and fallback channel with scoped optional upgrades. None automatically grants authority or determines whether the serving logic is agentic or deterministic. [S10, S12–S16]

## 7. Fulfillment and reversible specialization

A dispatcher selects among acceptable realizations according to the request, current dependencies, quality, cost and latency. A novel request may require intelligent interpretation; a stable repeated operation may use direct software; a mixed request may combine them.

The optimizer observes actual use, proposes a bounded improvement, validates it and activates it within existing authority. Its goal is useful fulfillment, not maximum generated code or minimum latency alone.

Withdrawal preserves capability disposition and accepted information. A fallback must meet the relevant promise. A material change to the meaning or effects is a contract revision, not an invisible optimization.

## 8. Human sovereignty and representation

Human decisions establish the permitted operational space. Agents can perform many lower-level actions within that space without seeking a repeated instruction for each step. They should escalate material ambiguity, reserved effects and authority conflicts.

The architecture also needs to account for interests. A representative may depend on a provider whose economic incentives differ from the principal's. The conversation's Personal Intelligence Fiduciary idea points to loyal representation as a complementary institutional question. It is not solved by a message format or by calling an agent personal. [S01]

Useful sovereignty includes understandable delegation, source access, practical recovery and the ability to replace actors. Technical availability alone does not establish these conditions.

## 9. A minimal reference experiment

Select one read-only capability and an authorized source set. Preserve its originals, define meaningful results and offer two interaction forms. Serve requests through a general interpretation route and one conventional route where available.

Measure outcomes and observed demand. Specialize one repeated pattern, then compare it with the original route on new and exceptional cases. Test a source revision, denied scope, implementation withdrawal and reconstruction of the relevant derived state.

This experiment establishes a bounded mechanism. Wider deployment, state-changing capabilities, public interfaces and market interaction require their own evidence and applicable authority. They should not be claimed on the basis of the read-only experiment.

## 10. Evaluation and unresolved research

The architecture should be assessed through semantic fidelity, useful completion, total cost, human effort, permission preservation, freshness, portability and recovery. Each dimension can reveal failure hidden by an impressive first demonstration.

Open questions include interoperability across different terminologies, cost-effective validation of generated realizations, evolving delegation, conflict among principals and the economics of long-term support.

The contribution is a composable model whose components can be independently useful. Information supplies continuity, shared meaning supplies coherence, human decisions establish freedom, and adaptable interaction and execution serve the need. This is the connected synthesis attributed to Loikkanen, presented as an invitation to implementation, comparison and critical testing.

# Liquid Software: The Economics of Execution — Version 3.0
URL: https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/economics-of-execution/v3/
Status: publication-candidate
Conceptual source: Valto Loikkanen

# Liquid Software: The Economics of Execution — Version 3.0

*A framework for choosing, materializing, adapting and dissolving implementations in an intelligence-native world.*

Conceptual source: **Valto Loikkanen**. The supplied research whitepaper is **version 3.0, dated 27 November 2026**: 33 pages, 31 chapters and 19 figures. Its cover and references explicitly identify AI-assisted synthesis and research. This overview and its calculation notes are additional AI-assisted editorial work.

This edition expands the [nine-page version 2.0](https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/economics-of-execution/). It is a proposed companion to *Beyond the Constraints of Software*. Its printed edition date is established; conceptual origin and website publication dates are separate matters. The framework, numerical scenarios and maturity spectrum remain proposals without empirical validation of the complete approach.

## What should exist?

Faster code generation changes the cost of producing software. The paper asks an additional question: when does the underlying need require a dedicated implementation at all?

A capability can combine general-purpose reasoning, existing software, skills, exact functions, declared rules, models and APIs. The economically meaningful unit can be a constituent of a larger activity. Selecting one realization does not require rebuilding the entire application or using one model for every step.

The objective is expected cumulative net value over time within requirements for accepted outcomes, quality, reliability, privacy, safety and authority. Runtime price alone is sufficient only when outcomes, timing and relevant risks are comparable. Stable software, existing SaaS, manual fulfillment and retaining the current system remain legitimate alternatives.

## Read the whole source

The [original 33-page PDF](https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/economics-of-execution/v3.0.pdf) retains all supplied bytes and figures. The [complete page-separated transcription](https://valto.github.io/liquid/whitepapers/economics-of-execution/v3/text/) retains all extracted wording, including references and AI attribution. Text extraction does not reproduce diagram geometry; consult the PDF for visual meaning.

The original v2 PDF, transcription and landing page remain at their existing addresses. Neither economics edition replaces the original umbrella or renumbers the sixteen drafts. The separately named *AI Maturity, Maturity Bias and Informed Selection* paper and Economics v1 were not supplied. Reading the maturity chapter in v3 does not establish access to that separate paper.

## Coverage of the expanded edition

| Pages | Chapters | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–2 | Cover and contents | Edition, conceptual source, AI attribution and chapter map. |
| 3–8 | 1–6 | Enduring information and authority; software-first and agent-first operating models; qualified car, humanoid, robot, road and house analogies; entity-level amortization and a reversible continuum. |
| 9–14 | 7–12 | Lifecycle cost, break-even analysis, distinct adoption and failure measures, evidence-driven investment, real options, forward and reverse transitions, time and opportunity cost. |
| 15–18 | 13–16 | Six-month cumulative value, flexibility loss, moving thresholds and attributable hosted-versus-owned model costs. |
| 19–21 | 17–19 | Modularity costs, capability contracts and a worked procurement composition. |
| 22–25 | 20–23 | Purposeful information processing, retrieval investment, stabilization and retirement, and a scenario-weighted discounted objective. |
| 26–28 | 24–26 | Decision-maker blind spots, understanding versus experience versus implementation, an eight-step protocol, a decision record and mixed capability portfolio. |
| 29–33 | 27–31 | Governance, research agenda, lineage, glossary, conclusion and nine references. |

## What v3 makes more explicit

**Serve, observe and invest selectively.** Where an acceptable initial path exists, serving a need can reveal demand and exceptions before major construction. Options to defer, expand, change or abandon investment can have value. Waiting has costs too: urgent capacity and hard requirements may justify upfront specialization. Reward business outcomes and avoided waste rather than application or agent counts.

**Compare sequences.** A strategy may serve now with an agent, build a validated function in parallel, then specialize if future demand justifies it. Each stage and transition must be feasible. Early fulfillment does not prove that a later build is worthwhile.

**Distinguish constraints.** Stable safety, privacy and authority controls may be necessary. Incidental workflow limitations can be reconsidered. Flexibility has economic value when future changes are plausible and consequential; architectural elegance alone is not a valuation method.

**Amortize at the actual boundary.** Market demand can repay a vendor's shared product. A private implementation depends on attributable entity use, including reuse across activities. Buying or renting existing tools can still be the best choice.

**Count the cost of adaptability.** Interfaces, dependencies, validation, change reviews and the optimizer itself consume resources. Retain stability when change brings no material benefit. Retirement must preserve commitments and source evidence or explicitly revise the commitment through appropriate authority.

## Checked illustrative calculations

These are supplied assumptions, not market prices, deployment results or forecasts. Arithmetic checks do not validate the economic model.

| Example | Assumptions | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Break-even, p. 10 | Fixed software €1,200; agent €2.50/use; software €0.10/use | Equal cost at 500 future executions. At 100 uses: €250 versus €1,210; at 1,000: €2,500 versus €1,300. |
| Six-month contribution, p. 15 | Both build a €12,000 module. Months 4–6 net €4,500/month; the agent path additionally nets €2,500/month in months 1–3 | Software-first €1,500; agent-first then module €9,000; difference €7,500. |
| Moving thresholds, p. 17 | Fixed €1,200 and software €0.10/use; agent €2.50, €1.30 or €0.50 | Thresholds 500, 1,000 and 3,000. Software-production costs can change too. |
| Retrieval, p. 23 | Preprocessing/upkeep €1,300, then €0.01/retrieval; on-demand €0.20/retrieval | At 1,000: €1,310 versus €200. At 10,000: €1,400 versus €2,000. Continuous crossover 6,842.105…; the first whole count favoring preprocessing is **6,843**. |
| Reused function, p. 28 | Fixed €900; agent €0.40/use; function €0.02/use | At 6,000: €2,400 versus €1,020, saving €1,380. At 1,000: €400 versus €920; a new build does not repay itself here. |

The source rounds the retrieval crossover to approximately 6,842. The whole-count note is editorial; original wording remains intact. Retrieval events need not be unique documents: the 10,000-document archive size is distinct from demand. Basic indexing and access controls are assumed equally available to both paths.

Past usage is sunk; thresholds concern remaining demand and future incremental investment. An already-built function needs a comparison of avoidable future costs rather than another construction charge. Released staff capacity is not automatically cash savings: identify conversion into avoided hiring, useful throughput or another accepted benefit.

Positive discounting reduces the present value of a fixed future cash flow; earlier receipt can improve value relative to later receipt. It does not make the same early cash flows worth more than their undiscounted sum.

## Maturity means informed selection

Page 26 distinguishes **understanding maturity**, **experiential maturity** and **implementation maturity**. Broader awareness can reveal more options while leaving a conventional deterministic service as the safest or most valuable choice.

V3 defines **maturity bias** as limitations to perceived alternatives arising from current understanding and experience. This expands the v2-derived explanation's warning against judging decision quality by position on a presumed implementation progression. The formulations are distinct and the revision is attributed explicitly.

The spectrum from traditional software through AI-enabled, agentic, agent-first and AI-native operations, plus unknown further paradigms, is conceptual. It is not a validated personal assessment or an instruction to maximize agents. Practical exposure can inform selection; an AI-written application or a permanently packaged agent does not prove wider alternatives were considered.

## Reference audit

References 1–8 are retained from v2. Their existing captures and read assessments are reused; no fresh full reading of those originals is claimed. Reference 9 connects the existing public collection. The bibliography adds lineage rather than new independent empirical support.

1. [Pendo's 2019 Feature Adoption Report](https://www.pendo.io/resources/the-2019-feature-adoption-report/): vendor cohort and extrapolated R&D estimate; main report and methodology previously read. Underused features are not necessarily valueless.
2. [GAO-26-107737, Technology Modernization Fund](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-26-107737/index.html): highlights, completed-project findings and relevant methodology previously read; particular portfolio and savings eligibility, no universal failure rate.
3. [GAO-11-53](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-11-53): previously inaccessible; a fresh web retrieval returned no readable content. A relevant passage of [Senate Report 114-162](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CRPT-114srpt162/html/CRPT-114srpt162.htm) previously corroborated ECSS cancellation and expenditure, not every later GAO status detail.
4. [UK supply-chain IT research](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/use-of-it-systems-by-uk-businesses-for-managing-supply-chain-data/use-of-it-systems-by-uk-businesses-for-managing-supply-chains): relevant qualitative adoption, removal and methodology sections previously read; mechanisms rather than prevalence or a standard cost multiplier.
5. [Washington Post, D.C. payroll computers, 14 October 2002](https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2002/10/14/34-million-fails-to-fix-dc-payroll-computers/a2a7fda1-6f95-4c42-ad2d-082e53e02e55/): original remains unread after unsuccessful access. Amount and cost composition remain source-attributed claims.
6. [Stanford AI Index 2025 R&D highlights](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/research-and-development): main highlights previously read; November 2022–October 2024 MMLU-level inference prices, not full-agent cost or a forecast.
7. [CRD](https://valto.github.io/crd/): main overview previously read; capability descriptions confer neither permission nor guaranteed interchangeability.
8. [MDIL/Kide](https://mdil.ai/): visible vendor overview previously read; architectural claims without an independent comparative benchmark or verified production-availability assessment.
9. [Liquid Software collection](https://valto.github.io/liquid/): existing public conceptual lineage; same-origin work, not independent corroboration.

The [Capability Economics explanation](https://valto.github.io/liquid/concepts/capability-economics/) develops the objective, scenarios, practical record and tests. [Adaptive Information Retrieval](https://valto.github.io/liquid/concepts/adaptive-information-retrieval/) develops purposeful processing. The research agenda asks for matched capability comparisons, actual lifecycle costs, quality, transition burden, realized value and responses to change.

## Publication status

This v3 page, original and transcription are a local publication candidate. The printed date does not establish a website release date. Publication and proposed CC BY 4.0 terms await applicable owner approval; published v2 retains its recorded grant.

 Liquid Software
 The Economics of Execution

 A framework for choosing, materializing, adapting and
 dissolving implementations in an intelligence-native
 world.


   Intelligence is the default capability. Software is an optimization.

LIQUID SOFTWARE / ECONOMICS OF EXECUTION                                                           V3.0 · NOVEMBER 2026




 READING MAP



 Contents
 Read sequentially for the full argument, or use the chapters independently. The public Liquid Software
 collection supplies the wider architectural context.

 01 Executive thesis · 3                                      17 Modularity · 19

 02 Introduction and scope · 4                                18 Capability contracts · 20
